MERRILL v. BECKWITH, 163 Mass. 503 (1895). The defendant, a resi dent of New York, exercised an option to buy the island of Nashawena in Massachusetts from the plaintiff, who filed a bill for specific performance. 

Service was made by publication, and by delivery of a copy to the committee of the property of the defendant in New York, where he had been adjudged a lunatic. A Massachusetts statute provided that when a person seized or possessed of real estate, or an interest therein, upon a trust, express or implied, was insane or out of the Commonwealth, and when in the opinion of the court it was fit that a sale should be made of such estate, or a conveyance should be made in order to carry into effect the objects of the trust, the court might by decree appoint some suitable person in the place of the trustee to convey as directed by the decree. The bill was dismissed. After quoting the statute and citing previous Massachusetts cases thereunder [see p. 75, n. 2, supra], LATHROP, J., said (p. 505): “. . . where one agrees to sell and the other to buy, there is correctly speaking no trust created, but merely a contract of sale and purchase of which a court of equity will under certain circumstances decree a specific performance.' 

But where the person agreeing to purchase has been allowed by the owner to enter upon the land and make improvements, there is a trust created in his favor. ..

However this may be, we are of opinion that the statute is not applicable to a person who has agreed to purchase; and that the court has no power under it to compel him to accept a conveyance, where the court cannot bind him personally by its decree."

PROBLEM CASES: 

1. In an equity suit begun by personal service, A was ordered to execute a deed of domestic land to B with specified trusts, within a certain time. A executed a deed to B after the time named, in terms slightly variant from the language of the decree. A statute provides that if the party ordered to make a conveyance does not comply by the time appointed, then the decree shall have the same effect as if the conveyance had been executed. Does B hold under the terms of the deed or of the decree? Price v. Sisson, 2 Beas. (13 N. J. Eq.) 

168, 172 (1860). 

2. V, a resident of Kansas, mortgaged Kansas land to M and then made a contract to convey the land to P by warranty deed. P sued for specific performance, serving V personally, and obtained a decree in conformity with the Kansas statute ordering V to make "a deed of conveyance" to P and declaring that in the event of V's failure to do so the decree should "stand as and for such conveyance." V executed no deed, but P paid the agreed price and obtained title and possession by virtue of the decree. M brought an action to foreclose the mortgage, joining P and V. P contended that if he should be compelled to pay off M, V should be liable for the amount of the mortgage as a warrantor. In Kansas a contract to make a deed implies the usual covenants of warranty. Is V liable to P? v. Golden, 96 Kan. 668 (1915), noted in 29 Harv. L. Rev. 770. 

3. In the preceding case suppose that V had been a non-resident, served only by publication in the specific performance suit, but personally served in the foreclosure suit. Would this affect his liability as a warrantor? 

4. P sued V, a resident, in state X for specific performance as to X land, serving V personally. The lower court rendered a decree, under a vesting statute, vesting all V's title in P and awarding P a writ of possession. P took pos-

The contract specified the prices as $20,000 for the patent, $5000 for the unpatented invention, and $5000 for the tools and patterns. B sues A in state Y for specific performance of the contract, paying $30,000 into court. A was served by publication and by delivery of a copy of the summons and complaint to him at his residence in X. Both X and Y have statutes applicable to personal property, authorizing such service in a specific performance suit against a non-resident and authorizing the court in its decree to appoint a master to execute a conveyance. Should the contract be enforced in whole or in part? See Ebsary Gypsum Co. v. 

Ruby, 256 N. Y. 406 (1931), and other patent cases cited supra, p. 88n. 

9. Bill for specific performance of a contract to convey domestic land gainst V, a non-resident, served by publication. P obtained a decree ordering to execute a deed. By statute this decree operated as a conveyance if V did not comply. V did not appear in the suit or execute the deed, but shortly after the decree he came into the state and was imprisoned for contempt. He eeks discharge on habeas corpus, maintaining the order of commitment to 

De void. Is he entitled to discharge? 

10. Bill by P to remove cloud on Illinois land against D, served in New York here D resided. D did not appear in the lower court. Decree for P in acordance with prayer of bill, with personal judgment against D for costs. D hen appeared and appealed as to costs. Should the decree be reversed, and ho should pay the costs of the appeal? Cloyd v. Trotter, 118 Ill. 391 (1886).

11. Suit in New Jersey against L, a Pennsylvanian, for specific performance of contract to lease New Jersey land. L was personally served in New Jersey, and a decree was made ordering him to appear in court on a day named and execute a lease. L failed to come, and returned to Pennsylvania. Thereupon, without further notice to L to appear, the court decreed that L was bound by all the covenants in the lease as fully as if executed by him; and that L was enjoined from ever denying that he had executed the lease, or defending any action at law on the lease on the ground that it had not been executed. L appealed. Should the decree be affirmed? Was V in contempt? Wharton v. 

Stoutenburgh, 39 N. J. Eq. 299 (1884), affg. 35 N. J. Eq. 266 (1882). 

12. L, a resident of Maryland, and N, a non-resident, gave a lease of Maryland land with a covenant for renewal for 99 years. The renewal lease was to contain personal covenants binding the lessors, their heirs, and assigns. P sued in Maryland for specific performance of the renewal covenant, serving L personally and N by publication. Should the court, acting under the Maryland appointive statute, direct a master to execute a new lease, or what relief should be given? Worthington v. Lee, 61 Md. 530, 541 (1883). 

13. A wife sued her non-resident husband, H, for divorce, serving him by publication. H had no property in the state, and did not appear. She obtained a final decree of divorce containing a provision ordering H to pay her alimony at the rate of $2000 a year. Later H came into the state, was personally served with a summons in the same cause, and appeared. A second decree for alimony at the same rate was then entered. Is either decree valid? Doeksen v. Doeksen, 202 Ia. 489 (1926), noted in 12 Ia. L. Rev. 195 and in 25 Mich. 

L. Rev. 527. 

14. A husband obtained a divorce in India on the ground of adultery. The wife was served personally, but the co-respondent, C, was served at his residence in England. The decree included an award of damages against C. The husband sues C in an English court on this decree. Can he recover? Phillips v. Batho, [1913] 3 K. B. 25. 

Interesting problems are also raised by Williamson v. Falkenhagen, 178 

Minn. 379 (1929), noted in 8 Tex. L. Rev. 597; Warlick v. Reynolds, 151 N. C. 

606 (1909); Husting Co. v. Coca-Cola Co., 194 Wis. 311 (1927), noted in 41 

Yale L. J. 1241.

PENN v. LORD BALTIMORE. 

CHANCERY, 1750. 

[1 Vesey Senior, *444.] 

[According to the Maryland charter of 1632 the northern boundary of Maryland began at that part of the Bay of Delaware . . . which lieth under the Fortieth Degree of North Latitude," and ran thence "in a right

Line, by the Degree aforesaid, into the true meridian of the first Fountain of the River Pottowmack." Basing their claim upon this description, the 

Lords Baltimore insisted that the fortieth parallel was the northern boundary of Maryland.

The charter issued to William Penn described the southern boundary of 

Pennsylvania as follows: 

"on the South by a Circle drawne at twelve miles distance from New Castle Northward and Westward into the beginning of the fortieth degre

CHAP. II] 

107 

PENN V. LORD BALTIMORE 

of Northern Lattitude, and then by a streight Line Westward . . . [5° in longitude]."

At this time the precise location of the fortieth parallel was not known. 

Penn was of the opinion that it was some miles farther south than it proved to be. In 1681-82 it was shown by observations to be considerably more than twelve miles north of Newcastle. [It passes slightly north of Philadelphia.] Penn made various proposals to locate the boundary considerably south of 40°, but Lord Baltimore insisted on that parallel as the boundary. 

The dispute was complicated by the execution of two deeds of feoffment by the Duke of York [afterwards James II], dated August 24, 1682, and conveying Delaware to Penn. By one of the deeds Penn was given the town of Newcastle and all the land lying within the compass or circle of twelve miles about that town, and by the other all the land on the Delaware River or Bay beginning twelve miles south of Newcastle and "extending south to the Whorekills, otherwise called Cape Henlopen." This territory, as it lay south of the fortieth parallel, was claimed as a part of Maryland by Lord Baltimore. Penn claimed that the Maryland charter conveyed only lands "hitherto uncultivated," and that Delaware had been early "cultivated" by the Dutch, to whom he traced his title. In 1685 the King approved a report of the Committee for Trade and Plantations recommending that the tract of land lying between the Delaware Bay and River and the Chesapeake Bay should be divided into "two equall parts by a line from the latitude of Cape hinlopen to the 40th degree of Northern latitude the western half to belong to Baltimore and the eastern half to Penn. Conflicting interpretations of this line depended on the location of Cape Henlopen. The Penns claimed the more southerly cape, and the Baltimores the more northerly one-the present Cape Henlopen. The line of 1685 was 

never run.

For upwards of half a century little advance was made toward the settlement of the controversy, although the need of a settlement became more important with the growth of the colonies and the consequent increase of strife in the disputed region. Finally, in 1732, the sons of William Penn and the great-grandson of the first Lord Baltimore executed in London. articles of agreement stipulating that the boundary should be a line beginning at the more southerly Cape Henlopen and running thence due west to the middle of the "Peninsula," thence along a tangent to a circle twelve miles from Newcastle to the tangent point, thence along a meridian to a parallel fifteen miles south of the most southerly part of Philadelphia, and thence westward along that parallel. There was, however, a proviso that if the meridian cut the circle (as was afterwards found to be the case), the boundary from the tangent point to the point at which the meridian cut the circle should be the arc of the circle.

The agreement of 1732 by no means ended the controversy. Commissioners who were appointed to run the line disagreed in 1733, and two years later the Penns filed a bill in chancery.¹]

The bill was founded on articles, entered into between the plaintiffs and defendant 10 May 1732, which articles recited several mat- 1 Reprinted, by permission, with some omissions and condensations, from Paullin and Wright, Atlas of the Historical Geography of the United States, 84 (1932). Plate 100C in this Atlas shows the claims of the parties, various provisional lines, and the final line.

ters as introductory to the stipulation between the parties, and particularly letters patent granted 20 June, 2 C. 1.1 by which the district, property, and government, of Maryland under certain restrictions is granted to defendant's ancestor his heirs and assigns: farther reciting charters or letters patent in 1681, by which the province of Pennsylvania is granted to Mr. William Penn and his heirs; and stating a title to the plaintiffs derived from James Duke of York, to the three lower countries by two feoffments, both bearing date 24 August 1682. The articles recite, that several controversies had been between the parties concerning the boundaries and limits of these two provinces and three lower counties, and make a particular provision for settling them by drawing part of a circle about the town of Newcastle, and a line to ascertain the boundaries between Maryland and the three lower counties, and a provision in whatever manner that circle and line should run and be drawn; and that commissioners should do it in a certain limited time, the final time for which was on or before 25 December 1733. There was beside a provision in the articles, that if there should be a want of a Quorum of commissioners meeting at any time, the party by default of whose commissioners the articles could not be carried into execution, should forfeit the penalty of £5000 to the other party: 2 and a provision for making conveyances of the several parts from one to the other in these boundaries, and for enjoyment of the tenants and landholders.

The bill was for a specific performance and execution of the articles: 

[The objections urged by the defendant included: ³] Eighthly, this court cannot make an effectual decree in the cause, nor enforce the execution of their own judgment.

LORD CHANCELLOR [LORD HARDWICKE]. I directed this cause to stand over for judgment, not so much from any doubt of what was the justice of the case, as by reason of the nature of it, the great consequence and importance, and the great labour and ability of the argument on both sides; it being for the determination of the right and boundaries of two great provincial governments and three counties; of a nature worthy the judicature of a Roman senate rather than of a single judge: and my consolation is, that if I should err in

my judgment, there is a judicature equal in dignity to a Roman senate that will correct it. 

It is unnecessary to state the case on all the particular circumstances of evidence; which will fall in more naturally, and very intelligibly, under the particular points arising in the cause. 

The relief prayed must be admitted to be the common and ordinary equity dispensed by this court; the specific performance of agreements being one of the great heads of this court, and the most useful one, and better than damages at law, so far as relates to the thing in specie; and more useful in a case of this nature than in most others; because no damages in an action of covenant could be at all adequate to what is intended by the parties, and to the utility to arise from this agreement, viz. the settling and fixing these boundaries in peace, to prevent the disorder and mischief, which in remote countries, distant from the seat of government, are most likely to happen, and most mischievous. Therefore the remedy prayed by a specific performance is more necessary here than in other cases: provided it is proper in all respects: and the relief sought must prevail, unless sufficient objections are shewn by defendant; who has made many and various for that purpose. . . .

The conscience of the party was bound by this agreement; and being within the jurisdiction of this court, which acts in personam, the court may properly decree it as an agreement, if a foundation for it. . .

As to the court's not inforcing the execution of their judgment; if they could not at all, I agree, it would be in vain to make a decree; and that the court cannot inforce their own decree in rem, in the present case: but that is not an objection against making a decree in the cause; for the strict primary decree in this court as a court of equity is in personam, long before it was settled, whether this Court could issue to put into possession in a suit of lands in England; which was first begun and settled in the time of James I. but ever since done by injunction or writ of assistant to the sheriff: but the court cannot to this day as to lands in Ireland or the plantations. 

In Lord King's time in the case of Richardson v. Hamilton, Attorney- 

General of Pennsylvania, which was a suit of land and a house in he town of Philadelphia, the court made a decree, though it could not be inforced in rem. In the case of Lord Anglesey of land lying n Ireland, I decreed for distinguishing and settling the parts of the state, though impossible to inforce that decree in rem, but the arty being in England, I could inforce it by process of contempt personam and sequestration, which is the proper jurisdiction of his court. I am of opinion therefore to decree a specific performance of this greement.

"" 1

MARSHALL, C. J., in MASSIE v. WATTS, 6 Cranch 148, 158 (U. S. 1810) 

(suit in United States Circuit Court in Kentucky by holder of prior equity in Ohio land to compel resident of Kentucky to convey legal title; decree for plaintiff): " where the defendant in the original action is liable to the plaintiff, either in consequence of contract, or as trustee, or as the holder of a legal title acquired by any species of mala fides practised on the plaintiff, the principles of equity give a court jurisdiction wherever the person may be found, and the circumstance, that a question of title may be involved in the inquiry, and may even constitute the essential point on which the case depends, does not seem sufficient to arrest that jurisdiction." The effect of this decree in Ohio was considered in Watts v. Waddle, 6 Pet. 389, 400 (U. S. 1832).

It is well recognized that jurisdiction exists to order a resident to convey foreign property by way of specific performance of a contract, performance of an express trust, or restitution of property obtained by fraud, at least when such a ground would furnish, as it usually would, a basis for similar relief in a suit at the situs of the property. See Beale, " Equitable Interests in 

Foreign Property," 20 Harv. L. Rev. 382 (1907), and Messner, "The Jurisdiction of a Court of Equity over Persons to Compel the Doing of Acts 

Outside the Territorial Limits of the State," 14 Minn. L. Rev. 494, 506 (1930), who present conflicting views on the difficult problem whether conveyances of foreign property should be ordered on other grounds than the three mentioned above, especially when the plaintiff's claim to the property would not be enforceable in the courts at the situs of the property. 

The problem is illustrated by the cases immediately following. See also 159

113 a money judgment against the plaintiff in the island of St. Christopher in a suit begun by nailing a copy of the writ and summons at the courthouse door. He levied execution on land of the plaintiff in the island worth £20,000, which was sold for £2000 to the defendant. The proceedings were regular by the law of the colony. Held, on repayment of the debt with expenses and interest, the defendant must reconvey the land, which will be considered in equity as taken for security only. ARDEN, M. R., said (p. 182): "I admit, I am bound to say, that according to those laws a creditor may do this. To that law he has had recourse, and wishes to avail himself of it: the question is, whether an English Court will permit such an use to be made of the law of that island or any other country. [Arglasse v. Muschamp and other cases] clearly shew, that with regard to any contract made or equity between persons in this country respecting lands in a foreign country, particularly in the British dominions, this Court will hold the same jurisdiction, as if they were situated in England. 

Therefore without affecting the jurisdiction of the Courts there, or questioning the regularity of the proceedings as in a Court of law, or saying, that this sale would have been set aside either in law or equity there, I have no difficulty in saying, . . . that this creditor . . . has gained an advantage, which neither the law of this nor of any other country would permit. I will lay down the rule as broad as this: this Court will not permit him to avail himself of the law of any other country to do what would be gross injustice. It is said, what if the sale had been to a third person? I am glad, I have not to determine that. A third person might have a great deal more to say, than this Defendant can. He might say, the law of the island authorizes a lottery; and having bid he has a right to retain it. But this Defendant has no such right except for the purpose of paying himself the debt." NORRIS v. CHAMBRES, 29 Beav. 246 (1861). Bill against the directors of an English corporation operating a mine in Prussia to recover money advanced to the company's agent and claiming a lien on the mine for that sum. 

The defendants were English directors, who were not personally accountable. The agent was not within the jurisdiction. The bill was dismissed. 

ROMILLY, M. R., said (pp. 253-256): "I am referred in support of this demand to the case of Penn v. Baltimore, and that class of cases which establishes that when a Plaintiff in England has an equitable money demand against a Defendant also residing here, this demand will be enforced by the Courts here, not merely against the Defendant personally, but, if the circumstances of the contract or dealings between the parties justify it, by the declaration of a lien against the real property of that Defendant out of the jurisdiction of the Court, and even, in some cases, by the appointment of a Receiver. Those cases have certainly, as Mr. Justice Story observes,¹ gone 

1 Story's Conflict of Laws, 791 (2d edit.).-REP. This. reference is prob ably to the second English edition, and apparently means the following passage (in § 544 of the American editions), discussing Penn v. Lord Baltimore, Lord Cranstown v. to the full extent of the assertion of jurisdiction of this Court, and they are always encumbered with this difficulty: - that the declaration of this decree may be a mere brutum fulmen, incapable of being practically enforced against the Defendant. Still, if the Plaintiff is entitled to it, this Court must give him the decree, as he asks for it, and then leave him to make it available or not, as he can, in a foreign country. 

I am not disposed however to go a step further than those cases warrant and demand. On examining them, I find that in all of them a privity existed between the Plaintiff and Defendant; they had entered into some contract or some personal obligation had been incurred moving directly from the one to the other. In this case, I cannot find that anything of that sort exists. 

If the owner of an estate in Prussia mortgage that estate to an Englishman, it is new to me, that the Courts of Equity in this country will administer, as between those persons, the law obtaining in England with relation to mortgages, and foreclose or direct a sale of the Prussian estate, if payment be not made of the amount due. 

But even, in so stating the case as a case of mortgage, I put it too favorably for the Plaintiff, for in that case, there would be a privity and personal contract between the parties, which here there is not. The facts of the case either constitute a valid hypothecation on the mine of the Defendants in Prussia in favor of the Plaintiff, or they do not. If they do, it is in Prussia, and the Courts of Law in that country, that this hypothecation is to be enforced; if they do not, I cannot make that a charge on immoveable property in Prussia which the law of Prussia treats as being no charge upon or hypothecation of the land itself. 

In the cases cited, the equity between the parties was complete, the Plaintiff was entitled to a decree to compel the Defendant personally to pay him a sum of money. ... But in this case, the very foundation is wanting, for independently of the lien which this Court is asked to declare, if needed, and which it is not asked to create, there is no equity between the parties; here the Plaintiff is entitled to no decree against the 

Defendants for payment of any sum of money, nor is any such claimed, but the equity and relief sought begin and end with a prayer to make a certain transaction between other persons, one of whom is a stranger to the Plaintiff, an interest in an estate in Prussia, belonging to that stranger, and this independently of all personal equities attaching upon him." This decision was affirmed, 3 De G. F. & J. 583 (1861).

Exercise of jurisdiction. Even if a court of equity possesses the power to act in personam and compel the defendant to convey foreign property, this power will not be used if the court does not think such relief desirable under the circumstances. See the remarks of Holmes, J., infra, p. 123, nn. 1, 2.

HALL, J., in BLOUNT v. BLOUNT, 1 Hawks, 365, 377 (N. C. 1821) (refus ing to order executors to sell land in another state): "I think it will be admitted that a court of equity ought not knowingly to do a vain thing make a decree which it cannot enforce." 

DESCHAMPS V. MILLER, [1908] 1 Ch. 856. Suit by the legitimate son of a Frenchman to set aside an old settlement of land and chattels in Madras by the father upon a bigamous wife, on ground of violation of marital rights of the legal wife and hence of plaintiff. The defendants were the trustees under the Indian settlement. Neither the Indian administrator of the legal wife nor the beneficiary under the settlement was a party. The bill was dismissed. PARKER, J., said (p. 863): "The question is whether under these circumstances the Court ought to entertain jurisdiction. In my opinion the general rule is that the Court will not adjudicate on questions relating to the title to or the right to the possession of immovable property out of the jurisdiction. There are, no doubt, exceptions to the rule, but, without attempting to give an exhaustive statement of those exceptions, I think it will be found that they all depend on the existence between the parties to the suit of some personal obligation arising out of contract or implied contract, fiduciary relationship or fraud, or other conduct which, in the view of a Court of Equity in this country, would be unconscionable, and do not depend for their existence on the law of the locus of the immovable property. Thus, in cases of trusts, specific performance of contracts, foreclosure, or redemption of mortgages, or in the case of land obtained by the defendant by fraud, or other such unconscionable conduct as I have referred to, the Court may very well assume jurisdiction. But where there is no contract, no fiduciary relationship, and no fraud or other unconscionable conduct giving rise to a personal obligation between the parties, and the whole question is, whether or not according to the law of the locus the claim of title set up by one party, whether a legal or equitable claim in the sense of those words as used in English law, would be preferred to the claim of another party, I do not think the Court ought to entertain jurisdiction to decide the matter."

WICKS V. CARUTHERS, 13 Lea, 353 (Tenn. 1884). Bill in Tennessee to compel the conveyance of Mississippi land by a trustee thereof, who resided in Illinois and was served with a subpoena while temporarily in Tennessee. The bill was dismissed without prejudice to the plaintiff's rights against the land. FREEMAN, J., said (p. 364): ". . . the question remains, can this court enforce the right thus claimed, even if sustained? We take it, the land lying in another State is beyond our control, and the parties

must be impleaded in that jurisdiction, when a charge on realty is to be enforced. It is a quasi proceeding in rem against the land, and not against beneficiaries and trustees, who are necessary parties only to settle equities between them, in order to ascertainment of what the land is chargeable with, the land after all is alone to be charged and appropriated. 

It is true the trustee is before the court by source of process of the court in fact in this case, but is out of the jurisdiction, but that does not give jurisdiction over the land, the subject-matter on which the charge is to be enforced, nor enable the court to compel the trustee to sell or convey. 

Our decree ordering him to sell, would only give authority in Tennessee, and be waste paper, as soon as he crossed the line of Mississippi, probably, but as he is out of the jurisdiction he cannot be so ordered. A mere declaration of right which we could not enforce, is what a court could not do, a decree which we have no jurisdiction to execute, would be tristem [sic] fulmen and a useless form not in accord with the course of judicial proceedings nor the dignity of such tribunals." But see Mussina v. Belden, 6 Abb. 

Pr. 165, 174 (N. Y. 1858). Compare Michigan Trust Co. v. Ferry, 228 

U. S. 346 (1913), infra, p. 122; p. 123, n. 3; Wharton v. Stoutenburgh, 39 N. J. Eq. 299 (1884), supra, p. 106, Problem Case 11; Matteson v. Scofield, 27 Wis. 671, 677 (1871), infra, p. 118, Problem Case 6. See Griffith v. 

Langsdale, 53 Ark. 71, 74 (1890). Other cases are cited in Note, 35 Harv.

L. Rev. 611, nn. 13-22 (1922). As to the possibility of a writ of ne exeat in this situation, see supra, p. 111, n. 1. As to suits against non-resident owners of foreign land who have not been personally served, see supra, p. 87n., 3d paragraph.

WESTCHESTER MORTGAGE Co. v. GRAND RAPIDS & IONIA R. R. Co., 246 N. Y. 194 (1927). Action, under the New York Declaratory Judgment Act, for a declaration as to the validity and priority of an assignment to the plaintiff, as collateral for a note, of the defendant's interest in a trust fund (apparently personalty) held by a Rhode Island trust company, trustee under a Rhode Island will. The court had personal jurisdiction over the assignor and all assignees subsequent to the plaintiff. The controversy turned on the possibly usurious nature of the plaintiff's note. A declaration as to rights in the fund was refused. LEHMAN, J., said (p. 200): "When appeal is made to our courts for relief in a matter of which they have jurisdiction, they may, of course, determine as a question of fact what is the law of a foreign jurisdiction and then decree relief in accordance with the law so found. Here, after the Supreme Court has determined that the plaintiff is the owner of the note, and has a lien upon the interest of Van Rensselaer in the property in Rhode Island, it can grant the plaintiff no further relief. The plaintiff's rights to such property are not merely determined by the law of Rhode Island, but can be enforced only in the courts of Rhode Island. 

Only by resort to the courts of that State may the lien upon the property in Rhode Island be foreclosed. Until then the declaratory judgment would be without practical effect. . . . We infringe upon the exclusive jurisdiction of courts of Rhode Island if we assume to dictate to them the extent to which they should enforce a lien upon property within that State. 

If that is the purpose and effect of the declaration made in this case, then it would seem clear that such a declaration should not have been made. ... It may perhaps be said that the purpose and effect of the declaratory judgment is not so much to bind the courts of the State of Rhode Island in

CHAP. II] 

117 

PROBLEM CASES 

the determination of the extent to which they may enforce a lien on property within that State as to preclude the parties from again litigating in that State an issue already determined here. Even if that be the result of the judgment rendered in this case, the fact still remains that the courts here have determined that issue without any purpose of granting relief here, and not as part of a declaration of 'rights' which may be made effective here without resort to the courts of a foreign sovereignty, or of 'legal relations,' with consequential result here between persons within the jurisdiction of our own courts. The plaintiff's rights against the property in 

Rhode Island are rights in rem. They can be enforced solely by the courts of Rhode Island. The Supreme Court has been asked to declare what the plaintiff's rights are. It has not been asked by the defendant. . . to declare any rights he may have to redeem or kindred rights. The declaration of the extent to which the courts of Rhode Island will enforce the plaintiff's rights has no purpose or effect, unless it be to remove to the courts of this State an issue which is properly determinable in an action to enforce rights in rem of which the courts of Rhode Island have exclusive jurisdiction.

If the courts of one jurisdiction have the power to declare rights which can be made effective only by appeal to the courts of another sovereignty, it is a power which in the interests of comity must be sparingly exercised. .. Perhaps where question of the law of this jurisdiction may be the determinative factor in an action in a foreign jurisdiction, our courts might declare the law of this jurisdiction as an aid to the foreign court." 

See comment in 41 Harv. L. Rev. 257; Braman v. Babcock, 98 Conn. 549 (1923).

PROBLEM CASES: 

1. The defendant agreed to buy land in Alberta from the plaintiff. Does a specific performance suit lie in Minnesota, where both parties reside? Kerr v. 

Nygren, 114 Minn. 268 (1911), noted in Ann. Cas. 1912C, 539. 

2. V agreed to sell land in state S to P. V died leaving an infant heir H. 

Has P any remedy against H in state F, where they both reside? Sutphen v. 

Fowler, 9 Paige, 280 (N. Y. 1841). See also Asberry v. Mitchell, 121 Va. 276 (1917); Durfee, Cases on Equity, 112n (1928). Would it be material that both state S and state F had vesting decree statutes? 

3. A and B agreed to exchange A's land in Michigan for B's land in Iowa. 

B was also to pay $2000 in cash. Deeds were executed on both sides and deposited at a bank, to remain until B paid the $2000. Without doing so, B fraudulently obtained from the bank the Michigan deed signed by A. B recorded the deed in Michigan, and then conveyed the Michigan land to C, who had notice of the fraud. C recorded his deed. All the parties resided in 

Illinois, which has a master's deed statute. A sued B and C to set aside the deed, serving them in Illinois. The lower court gave a decree that the Michigan deeds were null and void and should be surrendered for cancellation. B and 

C appealed. What decision? Cooley v. Scarlett, 38 Ill. 316 (1865).

4. V, a resident of Cuba, agreed to sell land in Florida for a specified sum to P, a resident of New York. V sent the deed to A, his agent in New York, but commanded him not to deliver the deed to P until he had paid a sum much larger than the price. P sued V and A for specific performance, and prayed an injunction to restrain A from sending the deed back to Cuba. A was personally served. V was duly notified in Cuba, but did not appear. Should P obtain any relief? Ward v. Arredondo, 1 Hopk. Ch. 213 (N. Y. 1824). See the comment in 69 L. R. A. 676 (1906). 

5. Suit in state X for specific performance in respect of land in state Y. 

The defendant vendor, a resident of X, was personally served. A statute of 

X provides that a decree for specific performance shall operate as a deed without any conveyance being executed by the vendor, and that such a decree shall be recorded in the county where the land lies. Does this statute bar relief? Hume v. Kirkwood, 216 Ala. 534 (1927), noted in 3 Ala. L. J. 143. 

6. D, a resident of Connecticut, while temporarily in Wisconsin, was served with a summons in a suit filed by P for specific performance of a contract to convey Wisconsin land. D put in an answer and contested the suit on its merits. Then he left Wisconsin permanently. Wisconsin has a vesting decree statute. Should jurisdiction be exercised? Matteson v. Scofield, 27 Wis. 671 (1871). Cf. Wicks v. Caruthers, 13 Lea, 353 (Tenn. 1884), supra, p. 115. 

7. A conveyed land in state X to B by a deed which passed title, but the mode of acknowledgment was so defective that the law of X prevented the deed from going to record as evidence of title against innocent purchasers. A is threatening to dispose of the land to others. A and B are residents of state 

Y. May B have any relief against A in that state? Frank v. Peyton, 82 Ky. 

150 (1884). 

8. A statute of state F requires that actions for the recovery of real property or of an estate or interest therein, or for the determination in any form of such right or interest," shall be brought in the county where the land lies. V and P resided in state F. V agreed to sell to P land in state S. P sues 

V for specific performance in the county of V's residence in state F, serving him personally. V moves to dismiss the action for want of proper venue. What decision? Newton v. Bronson, 13 N. Y. 587 (1856). But see State ex rel.

Hunt v. Grimm, 243 Mo. 667 (1912) (with dissent; cloud on title); Goode, "Jurisdiction in Equity over Foreign Lands," 3 St. Louis L. Rev. 127 (1919). 

Other cases are collected in 10 Minn. L. Rev. 608 (1926); Note, 3 Ann. Cas. 

1004 (1906). 

9. In the preceding case suppose the land was situated in state F but not in the county of V's residence, where the specific performance suit was brought. 

What decision on the same motion? See Manley v. Carter, 7 Kan. App. 86 (1898); Munger v. Crowe, 219 Ill. 12 (1905). 

10. H removed from state N to state M and got a divorce in state M, serving his wife, W, by publication. W now files a bill in state M to set aside the divorce decree on the ground that it was obtained by H's fraud. Since H cannot be found in state M, he is served by publication as a non-resident. H appears specially and moves to vacate the service of summons, contending W's suit is in personam. Should the motion be granted? State ex rel. Sparrenberger v. District Court, 66 Mont. 496 (1923), noted in 33 A. L. R. 469. Would the result be the same if suit had been brought after H's death against H's second wife? Compare State v. Moore, 46 Nev. 65 (1922) (suit by state to set aside divorce decree for alleged fraud).

DESCHENES V. TALLMAN DESCHENES v. TALLMAN. 

COURT OF APPEALS, NEW YORK, 1928. 

[248 New York Reports, 33.] CARDOZO, CH. J. The complaint is for the foreclosure of a purchase-money mortgage. The answer is a counterclaim for breach of a covenant of seizin. Whether seizin was lacking is the question to be answered.

Plaintiffs sold the land to the defendant Francis Tallman in April, 1925. A predecessor in title was Miller & Lockwell, Limited, a

Canadian corporation. By a decree of the courts of the Province of 

Quebec, made in 1911, the corporation was adjudged insolvent, and its property, real and personal, was ordered to be sold by two liquidators duly appointed according to the laws of the Province. The liquidators conveyed the land to the plaintiffs, who thereafter sold to Tallman with covenant of seizin. The land is located in the city of New York. The defendants insist that title does not pass under a deed by foreign liquidators.

A second and confirmatory deed, made in December, 1926, is also the subject of attack. After the sale to Tallman, the plaintiffs procured the execution of a quitclaim deed by the Canadian corporation. This deed, made by the corporation to the defendant Francis 

Tallman, contains a recital that it is given "in confirmation of a deed " made by the liquidators," it being the opinion of the liquidators that this deed is necessary for the beneficial winding up of the party of the first part and they having requested the execution of the same." The statutes of Canada are to the effect that the corporate life survives the appointment of a liquidator until the winding up is finished, but that the powers of the directors cease "except in so far as the court or liquidator sanctions the continuance of the same." The defendants insist that the later deed, being made under compulsion, adds nothing to the first one, and leaves the title where it was.

The answer demands judgment for the cancellation of the purchase-money mortgage, the return of the cash payment, and reimbursement for the value of subsequent improvements. 

We think the counterclaim must fail.

There is no need to determine what effect would be given to the liquidators' deed considered by itself.¹ . . .

If the deed by the liquidators be assumed to be inoperative, there was none the less a conveyance of title upon delivery by the corporation of a confirmatory deed of grant. A judgment of a foreign 

1 The court's discussion of the relevant considerations with regard to the question thus left open is omitted.

court will not avail of its own force to transfer the title to land located in this State. It will not avail though a conveyance be executed by the sheriff or a master or other agent of the court in fulfillment of its mandate (Fall v. Eastin, 215 U. S. 1, 11; Carpenter v. Strange, 141 U. S. 87, 105; Watts v. Waddle, 6 Pet. [U. S.] 389). "The court, not having jurisdiction of the res, cannot affect it by its decree, nor by a deed made by a master in accordance with the decree" (Fall v. Eastin, supra). But the rule is different where the conveyance is executed by the owner, though he act under compulsion (Fall v. Eastin, supra, at p. 11; Watkins v. Holman, 16 Pet. 

[U.S.] 25, 57; Corbett v. Nutt, 10 Wall. [U. S.] 464, 475; Gardner v. 

Ogden, 22 N. Y. 327). The conveyance, and not the judgment, is then the source of title. As to this the law has been undoubted since 

Penn v. Lord Baltimore (1 Ves. Sr. 444). The distinction is between a judgment directed against the res itself, and one directed against the person of the owner, who acts upon the res. His deed transmits the title irrespective of the pressure exerted on his will.¹ 

The order of the Appellate Division and that of the Special Term should be reversed, with costs in the Appellate Division and in this court, and judgment ordered in favor of the plaintiffs for the relief demanded in the complaint. 

POUND, CRANE, LEHMAN, KELLOGG and O'BRIEN, JJ., concur; 

ANDREWS, J., not sitting.

Ordered accordingly.2 

PROBLEM CASES: 

1. Gulliver, a wealthy resident of state X, went to a foreign country, F, to visit his daughter, who had married S, a citizen of F. By the law of F, a father-in-law can be compelled to convey property, wherever situated, to his son-in-law sufficient to provide for the support of the latter. S sued Gulliver in F, serving him personally, and obtained a decree ordering Gulliver to convey to S an apartment-house in state X. He refused, was imprisoned for contempt, and eventually signed a deed to S, which S recorded in the land records of X. 

On his return home Gulliver sued in X to cancel the deed for duress, serving S by publication under statute. X also has a vesting decree statute. Should relief be given? See De Brimont v. Penniman, 10 Blatchf. 436 (Circ. Ct. S. D.

N. Y. 1873). Compare Fauntleroy v. Lum, 210 U. S. 230 (1908).

Gulliver was served with a complaint filed by N, under a statute of Q providing that a rich man, whether citizen or alien, shall convey to his poor neighbors such 1 The remainder of the opinion deals with technical questions as to what constitutes a breach of a covenant of seizin.

At the hearing it was proved that N lives in a miserable hovel behind Gulliver's two large houses, one empty, the other occupied by himself and a retinue of servants. The court of Q decreed that Gulliver should do equity by granting a ten-year lease of the empty house to N at a rent of $1 per annum. Gulliver was contumacious, and was sentenced to jail for contempt. After one look at the jail he executed the lease, and went home. He now sues N in state X to set aside the lease, serving N personally. What decree? See D'Arcy v. Lyle, 5 Binn. 441 (Pa. 1813).

NOTE ON RECOGNITION OF MONEY DECREES OF OTHER STATES 

Under the full faith and credit clause of the United States Constitution, a final judgment in a civil action at law must be recognized by the courts of sister states.¹ This does not require those courts to issue execution on the judgment. 3 Freeman, Judgments (5th ed.) § 1358 (1925). But the sister state must (1) consider the judgment as res adjudicata, and (2) allow the maintenance of an action on the judgment if it is for money. Freeman, op. cit., § 1451 ff. In Fauntleroy v. Lum, 210 U. S. 230 (1908), a Mississippi court was compelled to grant recovery on a Missouri money judgment, although the original cause of action was an agreement made in Mississippi and unenforceable there because of a statute expressly making it illegal. 

See also Kenney v. Supreme Lodge, 252 U. S. 411 (1920). 

A money decree has marked resemblances in its own jurisdiction to a judgment at law. What are its consequences in sister states?

PENNINGTON V. GIBSON, 16 How. 65 (U. S. 1853). Action of debt in the 

United States Circuit Court in Maryland, to recover the amount of a New York decree in equity for the payment of money. The defendant's demurrer was held properly overruled. DANIEL, J., said (p. 76): “We hold no doctrine to be better settled than this, that whenever the parties to a suit and the subject in controversy between them are within the regular jurisdiction of a court of equity, the decree of that court solemnly and finally pronounced, is to every intent as binding as would be the judgment of a court of law, upon parties and their interests regularly within its cognizance. It is true that, owing to the peculiar character of equity jurisprudence, there are instances of decisions by courts of equity which can be enforced only by the authority and proceedings of these courts. 

Such, for example, is the class of cases for specific performances; or wherever the decision of the court is to be fulfilled by some personal act of a party, and not by the mere payment of an ascertained sum of money. But this arises from the nature of the act decreed to be performed, and from the peculiar or extraordinary power of the court to enforce it, and has no relation whatsoever to the comparative dignity or authority between judgments at law and decrees in equity. We lay it down, therefore, as the general rule, that in every instance in which an action of debt can be maintained upon a judgment at law for a sum of money awarded by such judgment, the like action can be maintained upon a decree in equity which is for an ascertained and specific amount, 1 For the text of the full faith and credit clause, see infra, p. 128, n. 1. 

As to the effect of a judgment at law in merging the original cause of action, see Langdell, supra, p. 20. 

2 See pp. 38-49, 64–67, supra.

and nothing more; and that the record of the proceedings in the one case must be ranked with and responded to as of the same dignity and binding obligation with the record in the other." 

Did this case involve the full faith and credit clause?

The full faith and credit clause was held to apply to a decree for the unconditional payment of money in Sistare v. Sistare, 218 U. S. 1 (1910). 

Among numerous decisions allowing actions on money decrees of other jurisdictions, see supra, p. 40, nn. 1 and 2; Boyle v. Schindel, 52 Md. 1 (1879), supra, p. 44; Post v. Neafie, 3 Caines, 22 (N. Y. 1805), supra, p. 43. 

Compare Sadler v. Robins, 1 Camp. 253 (1808); Du Bois v. Seymour, 152 

Fed. 600 (C. C. A. 3d, 1907). 

Will a suit in equity lie on a money decree of another state? See Davis v. Headley, 22 N. J. Eq. 115 (1871); Bennett v. Bennett, 63 N. J. Eq. 306 (1901); Kent, J., dissenting in Post v. Neafie, supra, pp. 43-44; and the cases cited in Problem Case 2, infra, p. 124.

As to foreign money decrees as res adjudicata, see Smith v. Cowell, 41 

Colo. 178 (1907); Harrington v. Harrington, 154 Mass. 517 (1891); Mutual 

L. Ins. Co. v. Newton, 50 N. J. L. 571 (1888), supra, p. 38; Young v. Farwell, 165 N. Y. 341 (1901).

MICHIGAN TRUST Co. v. FERRY, 228 U. S. 346 (1913). D was appointed by a probate court in Michigan as executor of two estates. He moved to 

Utah, became incompetent, and was put under guardianship. Later a suit was brought by legatees and devisees in the Michigan probate court for D's removal and an accounting. Notice was given by publication and by service in Utah upon D and his guardians. The guardians appeared in 

Michigan by order of the Utah court and obtained the appointment of a guardian ad litem. Lawyers were retained and paid out of D's estate by order of the Utah court. An answer and cross-petition praying for affirmative relief were filed. At the end of various proceedings P was appointed administrator de bonis non of both estates, and D was declared indebted to the two estates for specified sums. The decrees of the Michigan probate court ordered D to pay these sums to P within sixty days. P sued D upon these decrees in the United States Circuit Court for the District of Utah, which sustained D's demurrers and entered judgments for D. These were affirmed by the Circuit Court of Appeals, on the ground that the Michigan court had only jurisdiction in rem over the assets of the estates, and could not render the money decrees in personam against D, because of want of personal service or voluntary appearance of D in Michigan and because the general guardians had no power outside Utah to bind his person or charge his Utah estate. 175 Fed. 667, 681. The Supreme Court (two judges dissenting) reversed the judgments, HOLMES, J., saying (pp. 353, 355, 356): "Ordinarily jurisdiction over a person is based on the power of the sovereign asserting it to seize that person and imprison him to await the sovereign's pleasure. But when that power exists and is asserted by service at the beginning of a cause, or if the party submits to the jurisdiction in whatever form may be required, we dispense with the necessity of maintaining the physical power and attribute the same force to the judgment or decree whether the party remain within the jurisdiction or not. This is one of the decencies of civilization that no one would dispute. It applies to Article IV, § 1, of the Constitution, so that if a judicial proceeding is begun with juris-

123 diction over the person of the party concerned it is within the power of a State to bind him by every subsequent order in the cause. It is true that it could not be enforced in Michigan while the defendant remained out of the State. But while the want of power to enforce a judgment or decree may afford a reason against entertaining jurisdiction, Giles v. Harris, 189 

U. S. 475, 488,¹ it has nothing to do with the validity of a decree when made. 

A decree in equity against a defendant who had left the State after service upon him and had taken all his property with him would be entitled to full faith and credit where he was found. The judgment of a court may be complete and perfect and have full effect independent of the right to issue execution.' Mills v. Duryee, 7 Cranch, 481, 485. See Kimball v. St. 

Louis & San Francisco Ry. Co., 157 Mass., 7, 8.2 ...

Jurisdiction is power, and the power of the Michigan court was not affected by the insanity of Ferry. The authority of the State to remove him and to require his account to be settled at the same time remained, and therefore, subject to any restrictions that might be imposed by the Fourteenth Amendment, it was for the State to determine how he should be represented and what steps should be taken to protect his rights." 3 

Foreign alimony decrees. Various difficult problems of conflict of laws and domestic relations are raised by a suit in one state upon the alimony 1 Bill in equity by an Alabama negro on behalf of himself and more than 5000 other negroes to require a county board of registrars to enrol the negroes as voters. Unless we are prepared to supervise the voting in that State by officers of the court, it seems to us that all that the plaintiff could get from equity would be an empty form." The bill was dismissed without prejudice to further proceedings by the plaintiff. Cf. Nixon v. Herndon, 273 U. S. 536 (1927); Nixon v. Condon, 286 U. S. 73 (1932).

The plaintiffs necessarily will be referred to the courts of Missouri to compel the defendant to respect their rights, in case compulsion is necessary. PROBLEM CASES: 

1. A Californian sued a resident of Massachusetts in equity in Rhode Island to compel the conveyance of trust land in that state, and for accounting of rents and profits. The defendant appeared. The Rhode Island court ordered a conveyance and the payment of $6800 for rents and profits. The defendant conveyed but did not pay. The Californian now sues in Massachusetts in quasi-contract to recover the rents and profits. The defendant sets up the 

Rhode Island decree. What should the trial judge do? Harrington v. Harrington, 154 Mass. 517 (1891). 

2. In a New York suit of an equitable nature to annul a marriage, with personal jurisdiction over both parties, the marriage was not annulled, but judgment was entered in favor of the wife for a specified sum due her for support pendente lite and counsel fees. The wife afterwards moved to Massachusetts, and sued her husband in equity in that state on this money judgment, obtaining personal service though he was still a resident of New York. Suits between husband and wife are not authorized in Massachusetts, with certain exceptions of equity suits involving property rights, which did not include this suit. Should the bill be dismissed? Weidman v. Weidman, 274 Mass. 118 (1931). See also Metzler v. Metzler, 8 N. J. Misc. 821, 151 Atl. 847 (1930). 

These cases are noted in 76 A. L. R. 1364; 11 B. U. L. Rev. 287; 31 Col. L. 

Rev. 316, 702; 29 Mich. L. Rev. 1071. Cf. Fauntleroy v. Lum, 210 U. S. 230 (1908). 

3. A sued B, then a resident of Mississippi, in a state equity court to recover slaves together with their hire. B appeared and made answer. After testimony had been taken on both sides, the bill was dismissed. B's attorney then withdrew his appearance and B moved to Texas. A then carried the case to the 

Mississippi appellate court, and, since B could no longer be personally served, gave notice of this proceeding for review by publication in conformity with a state statute. The appellate court reversed the decree below, and A obtained a decree for the return of the slaves, for their past hire, and for $200 a year

until their return. A then sued B at law in the United States District Court in Texas, setting forth the Mississippi decree. B's only defense was his removal from Mississippi before the proceedings for review. Verdict for A for the value of the slaves and their hire. B brings writ of error. What decision? Nations v. Johnson, 24 How. 195 (U. S. 1860). 

BURNLEY v. STEVENSON. 

SUPREME COURT, OHIO, 1873. 

[24 Ohio State Reports, 474.] 

Motion for leave to file a petition in error to reverse the judgment of the District Court of Pickaway county.

The original action was brought in the Court of Common Pleas of Pickaway county, by the plaintiffs in error, to recover from the defendant in error the possession of two undivided third parts of 606 acres of land, situate in said county, and being part of original survey No. 6,943, in the Virginia military district. The plaintiffs sought to recover in the right of the heirs of Gen. Charles Scott, to whom the land embraced in this survey had been conveyed by the 

United States by patent, in the year 1812.

The defendant, by way of defense, set up in his answer the following state of facts, to wit: That previous to the date of said patent, Gen.

Charles Scott, having received a warrant for 1,666% acres of land, for military services rendered by him in the Virginia line in the continental establishment, had employed one John Evans, a surveyor, to locate, survey, and obtain patents for him, on said warrant, on lands in the Virginia military district, and in consideration of the services of Evans in the premises, had agreed to convey to him one-fifth part of all the lands so to be located, surveyed, and patented; that Evans duly performed said services; that the lands embraced in survey 6,943, were part of the lands located, surveyed, and patented to Gen. Scott under said warrant; that it was further agreed between Scott and Evans, that the share of Evans under the contract should be selected from lands in said survey; that soon after the issuing of the patents to Scott, he died, without having conveyed to Evans the lands to which he was entitled under said contract. 

That afterward Evans filed his bill in chancery, in the Circuit Court of Fayette county, Kentucky (the same being a court of general equity jurisdiction), against the heirs and legal representatives of said Scott (being the same persons under whom the plaintiffs claim title), to compel the specific performance of said contract, by a conveyance to him of the lands to which he was entitled thereunder; that said court obtained jurisdiction of the persons of all said heirs, by service of process and by voluntary appearance; that upon the final hearing of said cause upon the bill, answers, and exhibits, to

wit, on the 2nd day of February, 1816, the court found the equity of the case in favor of Evans, and directed the defendants therein to convey to him the lands described in the petition of the plaintiffs below; that it was further decreed by said court, that in default of such conveyance by the defendants, one Robert Scott, a master commissioner of said court, should make such conveyance; and that afterward, in pursuance of said decree, said master commissioner, to wit, on the 28th of May, 1817, executed and delivered to said Evans a deed in fee simple for said lands.

The defendant in his answer further sets forth, that he has succeeded to all the rights and title of said John Evans in and to said lands, and avers that he and those under whom he claims, are now lawfully in possession thereof, and have so been in possession, claiming under said decree and the deed from said master, ever since the dates thereof.

To this defense the plaintiffs below filed their reply, to which the defendant demurred. The demurrer was sustained, to which ruling the plaintiffs excepted.

Judgment was therefore rendered in favor of the defendant below, which was afterward, on error, affirmed by the District Court. 

To reverse these judgments, this proceeding is now instituted. 

Plaintiffs in error admit that their reply in the court below was insufficient, if the above matters and things contained in the answer, constituted a good defense to the action.

MCILVAINE, J. The main proposition submitted in this case is, whether, under and by virtue of the decree of the Circuit Court of Kentucky and the master's deed made in pursuance thereof, or of either of them, such an estate or right was vested in John Evans as entitles the defendant, who has succeeded to all the rights of Evans, to the possession of the lands in controversy, as against the plaintiffs, whose claim of title is derived from the parties against whom the decree was rendered. 

1. The jurisdiction of the Circuit Court to pronounce the decree, is the first inquiry involved in this proposition. 

It appears from the record before us, that the Circuit Court of Kentucky which pronounced the decree, was a court of general equity jurisdiction; that some of the defendants in the cause were properly served with the process of the court, and that all others voluntarily appeared and submitted themselves to its jurisdiction, and that the subject-matter of the bill on which the decree was rendered, was the enforcement of a trust and the specific performance of a contract to convey lands situate in the State of Ohio. 

That courts exercising chancery powers in one state have jurisdiction to enforce a trust, and to compel the specific performance of a contract in relation to lands situate in another state, after having

CHAP. II] 

127 

BURNLEY V. STEVENSON 

obtained jurisdiction of the persons of those upon whom the obligation rests, is a doctrine fully settled by numerous decisions. Penn v. 

Lord Baltimore, 1 Ves. 444 [supra, p. 106]; Massie v. Watts, 6 

Cranch, 148; Penn v. Hayward, 14 Ohio St. 302, and cases therein cited. 

2. It does not follow, however, that a court having power to compel the parties before it to convey lands situated in another state, may make its own decree to operate as such conveyance. Indeed, it is well settled that the decree of such court can not operate to transfer title to lands situate in a foreign jurisdiction.¹ And this, for the reason that a judgment or decree in rem can not operate beyond the limits of the jurisdiction or state wherein it is rendered. And if a decree in such case can not effect the transfer of the title to such lands, it is clear that a deed executed by a master, under the direction of the court, can have no greater effect. 

Watts v. Waddle et al., 6 Pet. 389; Page v. McKee, 3 W. P. D. Bush, 135. The master's deed to Evans must therefore be regarded as a nullity.2

The next inquiry then is as to the force and effect of the decree rendered by the Circuit Court directing the heirs of Gen. Scott to convey the land in Ohio to Evans. This decree was in personam, and bound the consciences of those against whom it was rendered. 

1 Accord: Carpenter v. Strange, 141 U. S. 87, 105 (1891); Dull v. Blackman, 

169 U. S. 243 (1898); West Point Mining Co. v. Allen, 143 Ala. 547 (1905); 

Lindley v. O'Reilly, 50 N. J. L. 636, 640 (1888); Sutphen v. Fowler, 9 Paige, 280 (N. Y. 1841); Sharp v. Sharp, 65 Okla. 76, 78 (1916); Williams v. Williams, 83 Ore. 59, 62 (1917); Wilson v. Braden, 48 W. Va. 196, 198 (1900); Tennant's 

Heirs v. Fretts, 67 W. Va. 569, 571 (1910) (semble) [supra, p. 91, at 92]. See also Fire Assn. v. Patton, 15 N. M. 304, 309–312 (1910).

The same result follows even though the state of suit or the state where the land lies or both have statutes enabling a court of equity to pass legal title by decree. See Watts v. Waddle, 6 Pet. 389, 400 TU. S. 1832); Watkins v.

Holman, 16 Pet. 25, 57 (U. S. 1842); Guarantee Trust & Safe-Deposit Co. v. 

Delta & Pine-Land Co., 104 Fed. 5, 10 (C. C. A. 5th, 1900). 

Additional authorities are collected in Note, 67 Am. Dec. 97 (1885), and in 

21 C. J. 151, nn. 69, 70. 66 

2 Accord: Watts v. Waddle, 6 Pet. 389 (U. S. 1832); Fall v. Eastin, 215 U. S. 

1, 8 (1909); Cole v. Manning, 79 Cal. App. 55, 64 (1926) (semble); Page v. 

McKee, 3 Bush, 135, 139 (1867); Andler v. Duke, 45 B. C. 96, 103 (1931), affd. as to this aspect of the case in Duke v. Andler, [1932] Can. S. C. 724. But see Cooley v. Scarlett, 38 Ill. 316 (1865), where Lawrence, J., said (p. 320): 'If they [the defendants in a suit to set aside as fraudulent a conveyance of land in Michigan] go beyond the jurisdiction, the court can appoint a special commissioner to make the conveyance in their stead." See also Poole v. 

Koons, 252 Ill. 49, 54 (1911), holding it not error to provide, in a decree for specific performance of land in Arkansas, for the execution of a master's deed if the defendant failed to convey as ordered. Criticizing this decision in Note, 6 Ill. L. Rev. 545 (1912), Schofield says: "An Illinois master's deed of land in

Arkansas, or in any other state of the Union, or in a foreign country, is so much waste paper." Cf. Hart v. Sansom, 110 U. S. 151, 155 (1884) [supra, p. 76, at 

79]; Lipe v. Lipe, 327 Ill. 39, 45–46 (1927).

In it, the contract of their ancestor to make the conveyance was merged. The fact that the title which had descended to them was held by them in trust for Evans, was thus established by the decree of a court of competent jurisdiction. Such decree is record evidence of that fact, and also of the fact that it [had] become and was their duty to convey the legal title to him. The performance of that duty might have been enforced against them in that court by attachment as for contempt; and the fact that the conveyance was not made in pursuance of the order, does not affect the validity of the decree in so far as it determined the equitable rights of the parties in the land in controversy. In our judgment, the parties, and those holding under them with notice, are still bound thereby. 

3. Under our code of practice, equitable as well as legal defenses may be set up in an action for the recovery of land. The defendant in the court below set up this decree of the Circuit Court of Kentucky as a defense to the plaintiffs' action. That it did not constitute a good defense at law may be admitted, but we think, in equity, it was a sufficient defense.

The constitution of the United States declares that full faith and credit shall be given in each state to the records and judicial proceedings of every other state, and provides that Congress may prescribe the mode of proving such records and proceedings, and the effect thereof. By an act of May 26, 1790, Congress declared that the "records and judicial proceedings of the state courts," when properly authenticated, "shall have the same faith and credit given to them in every court within the United States, as they have, by law or usage, in the courts of the state from whence they are or shall be taken." When, therefore, a decree rendered by a court in a sister state, having jurisdiction of the parties and of the subject-matter, is offered as evidence, or pleaded as the foundation of a right, in any action in the courts of this state, it is entitled to the same force and effect which it had in the state where it was pronounced. Mills v. 

Duryea, 7 Cranch, 481; Hampton v. McConnell, 3 Wheat. 234; Mc- 

Gilvray & Co. v. Avery, 30 Vermont, 538. That this decree had the effect in Kentucky of determining the equities of the parties to the land in this state, we have already shown; hence the courts of this state must accord to it the same effect. True, the courts of this state can not enforce the performance of that decree, by compelling the conveyance through its process of attachment; but when pleaded in our courts as a cause of action, or as a ground of defense, it must be regarded as conclusive of all the rights and equities which were adjudicated and settled therein, unless it be impeached for fraud. 

See cases supra; also, Davis v. Headley, 22 N. [J. Eq.] 115; Brown v. 

1 U. S. Const., Art. IV, § 1: "Full faith and credit shall be given in each 

State to the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of every other State. 

And the Congress may by general laws prescribe the manner in which such acts, records and proceedings may be proved, and the effect thereof."
